question: Best fractional CRO for a Series B company?
body:
## Direct Answer

The best fractional CRO for a Series B company is an operator who has personally scaled revenue through the exact stage you are in now — roughly the two-to-ten-million to twenty-to-fifty-million ARR jump — and who can build repeatable go-to-market systems rather than just close deals personally. At Series B the mandate is not founder-led selling anymore; it is process, forecasting rigor, sales-marketing alignment, and a hiring engine that survives the leader's eventual exit. The "best" fit is therefore stage-specific, motion-specific (product-led, sales-led, or hybrid), and time-boxed to a clear 6-to-12-month transformation with defined handoff to a full-time hire.

Choosing a fractional Chief Revenue Officer at Series B is one of the highest-leverage decisions a scaling company makes, and also one of the easiest to get wrong. The temptation is to hire a big name from a household brand, but a leader who scaled revenue from two hundred million to a billion often has no muscle memory for the messy, under-instrumented reality of a thirty-person revenue org. This essay lays out what the role actually is at Series B, the concrete criteria that separate a transformational fractional CRO from an expensive advisor, how the economics compare to a full-time hire, and a practical vetting and engagement framework you can run this quarter.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do at Series B?

A fractional CRO is a senior revenue executive who works with your company part-time — commonly one to three days a week — on a fixed-term engagement, carrying real operational accountability for the revenue number rather than sitting on the sidelines as an advisor. The distinction matters. An advisor gives you a deck and a Slack channel; a fractional CRO owns pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, quota-setting, comp plan design, and the performance of the sales and marketing leaders who report into the function. They show up in your pipeline reviews, they sit in board prep, and they are measured on outcomes.

At Series B specifically, the job is a transformation mandate, not a maintenance one. By this stage you have proven that customers will pay and that some repeatable motion exists, but the machine is held together by founder heroics, a few star reps, and spreadsheets. The fractional CRO's real deliverable is a **system** — a documented sales process, a forecast the board can trust, a segmentation and territory model, a hiring scorecard, and the analytics to see leading indicators before they become missed quarters. Founders often mistake the need as "someone to bring in more deals." The deeper need is someone to make revenue predictable so the next $20M+ of ARR does not require the founder in every important call. For the mechanics of building that operating layer, see the RevOps foundations at [pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-system](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-system).

There is also a coaching dimension that is easy to undervalue. Many Series B companies have a first-time VP of Sales or a founder-turned-revenue-lead who has never managed managers. A strong fractional CRO spends as much time developing that person as running the number directly, because the entire point of the engagement is to leave behind a self-sufficient team. If the org gets worse the day the fractional leader walks out the door, the engagement failed regardless of the quarter's bookings.

## What should a Series B company look for in a fractional CRO?

The single most important filter is **stage-relevant scar tissue**. You want someone who has personally operated a revenue org through the specific inflection you are facing — turning early product-market fit into a scalable, forecastable engine. Ask candidates to name the ARR band they took a company from and to, and probe what broke along the way. A leader who only knows the enterprise machine at massive scale will over-engineer your thirty-person team; a leader who has only worked in seed-stage chaos will not know how to install the rigor a board now expects. The best fractional CROs have done the two-to-ten into twenty-to-fifty transition more than once and can tell you exactly which quarter the wheels come off and why.

Second is **motion match**. A product-led growth company with a self-serve funnel and a small expansion sales team needs a fundamentally different leader than an enterprise sales-led company running six-figure deals with twelve-month cycles. The comp plans, the metrics, the hiring profiles, and even the CRM architecture diverge sharply. When you interview, force the candidate to describe your motion back to you and explain how they would instrument it — vague answers here are disqualifying.

Third is **systems literacy over personal selling**. It is tempting to hire the charismatic closer, but at Series B your bottleneck is not the leader's rolodex — it is the absence of a repeatable process. Look for evidence they have built forecasting cadences, defined a sales methodology, designed onboarding ramps, and instrumented a funnel. The evaluation flow below captures the sequence most well-run Series B searches follow.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Define the mandate and stage] --> B[Screen for stage relevant experience]
    B --> C[Verify motion match PLG or sales led]
    C --> D[Test systems and forecasting skill]
    D --> E[Reference check with real operators]
    E --> F[Run a paid pilot sprint]
    F --> G[Set 90 day and 6 month goals]
    G --> H[Plan the full time handoff]
```

Fourth, insist on **references from people who reported to them**, not just the CEOs who hired them. A leader can charm a board and still demoralize a sales floor. The reps and the sales managers who lived under the person's cadence will tell you whether the systems actually worked and whether the team got better. Weight those conversations heavily. Deeper vetting mechanics live in the go-to-market hiring guide at [pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-leadership-hiring](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-leadership-hiring).

## Fractional versus full-time CRO: which does Series B need?

The honest answer for many Series B companies is fractional first, full-time later — and the reason is both economic and strategic. A full-time CRO at this stage commands a senior executive package plus meaningful equity, and hiring one prematurely locks you into a single bet before you even know exactly what kind of leader the scaled org will need. A fractional engagement lets you install world-class thinking now, prove out the operating model, and defer the permanent, expensive commitment until the role is well-defined and the company has grown into it.

The strategic argument is subtler. At Series B the revenue function is still being invented. Hiring a permanent CRO to invent it, then discovering the company needs a different profile to *run* it at scale, is a common and painful mis-hire — one that costs a year and a lot of trust. A fractional CRO can architect the system and then explicitly design and recruit their own full-time successor, which is a far lower-risk path than betting the whole function on one permanent hire made under pressure. The best fractional engagements are structured from day one to end in a clean handoff.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Series B revenue gap] --> B{Is the motion defined?}
    B -->|No| C[Fractional CRO to build the system]
    B -->|Yes and stable| D[Full time CRO to scale it]
    C --> E[Design forecasting and comp and hiring]
    E --> F[Recruit and onboard full time successor]
    F --> D
```

That said, fractional is not always right. If your revenue motion is already well-defined and stable, if you are raising a large round explicitly to scale a known engine, or if the board demands a permanent revenue leader for credibility with enterprise buyers, a full-time hire may be the correct call. The decision hinges on how much *invention* versus *execution* the next twelve months require. Invention-heavy situations favor fractional; pure scale-up execution favors full-time. For a fuller treatment of the sequencing, the revenue leadership stack breakdown at [pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leadership-stack](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leadership-stack) walks through when each role should enter the org.

## Where do you find a great fractional CRO, and how do you vet one?

There is no single marketplace that reliably surfaces the best fractional CROs, which is why sourcing is itself a skill. The strongest channel is your investor network. Series B firms have portfolios full of companies that have made this exact hire, and a warm introduction to a fractional CRO who already delivered for a comparable portfolio company is worth more than any cold search. Ask your lead investor and your board members directly: "Who is the best fractional revenue leader you have watched actually transform a portfolio company at our stage?" The specificity of that question filters out generic recommendations.

Beyond investors, look at operator communities and specialized fractional-executive networks, but treat platform listings as a starting point rather than an endorsement. The best fractional CROs are frequently fully booked and travel by referral; the ones aggressively marketing themselves are not automatically worse, but the ratio of talkers to operators is higher in open marketplaces, so your vetting bar has to rise accordingly. When you evaluate candidates, run a structured process rather than a series of impressed conversations.

Concretely, a rigorous vetting sequence looks like this. First, a working session where you hand the candidate an anonymized slice of your actual pipeline data and ask them to diagnose it live — this instantly separates the operators from the framework-reciters. Second, backdoor reference checks through your own network, not just the references they provide. Third, a small **paid pilot** — a two-to-four-week diagnostic sprint where they audit your funnel, forecast, and team and deliver a written plan. The pilot is the single best predictor of the full engagement because it shows you their real work product and working style before you commit, and it costs a fraction of a bad multi-quarter hire. If a candidate resists a paid pilot, that itself is a signal.

Finally, get the commercial terms and the exit plan in writing before you start. Define the day-per-week commitment, the specific 90-day and six-month deliverables, the metrics you will judge success by, and — critically — the trigger and plan for transitioning to a full-time leader. The single most common failure mode is a fractional engagement with no defined endpoint that quietly becomes a permanent, expensive dependency the org never outgrows.

## What are the red flags and common mistakes when hiring a fractional CRO?

The most expensive mistake is hiring for **brand over stage fit** — recruiting someone whose logo impresses the board but whose entire career was spent at scale far beyond yours. These leaders reflexively install enterprise processes, layers of management, and tooling your thirty-person team cannot absorb, and they get frustrated by the ambiguity that is normal at Series B. Prestige is not the same as relevance. Weight recent, stage-adjacent operating experience above famous logos every time.

A second red flag is the **advisor in operator's clothing** — someone who wants the title and the retainer but not the accountability. If a candidate is vague about carrying a number, resists being measured on forecast accuracy, or wants to "advise the CEO" rather than run the function and its people, they are an advisor, and you should hire them (or not) on advisor terms and price. The whole value of a fractional CRO is operational ownership.

Third, watch for **over-commitment across too many clients**. A fractional executive juggling six or seven engagements cannot give any of them real operational attention. Ask directly how many clients they carry and how many days a week you are actually getting. Two or three serious engagements is plausible; a leader spread across many is selling you a name, not their time.

Other recurring mistakes: skipping the paid pilot and going straight to a long contract; failing to give the fractional CRO real authority over the sales and marketing leaders, which turns them into a suggestion box the team ignores; and never defining the handoff, so the "temporary" leader becomes permanent by inertia. Avoid these and the fractional CRO becomes exactly what Series B needs — a way to buy senior revenue expertise precisely when the company needs it most, at a fraction of the cost and risk of getting the permanent hire wrong.

## Related questions

### How much does a fractional CRO cost compared to a full-time one?
Fractional CROs are typically engaged on a monthly retainer tied to days per week, which is a meaningful fraction of a full-time CRO's total compensation and usually carries little or no equity. Get exact quotes from candidates; avoid budgeting off rumored numbers.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most Series B engagements run six to twelve months — long enough to install forecasting, process, and hiring systems and to recruit a full-time successor, short enough to force a clear endpoint. Open-ended engagements tend to drift into costly permanence.

### Can a fractional CRO also be the VP of Sales?
Rarely well. The CRO builds cross-functional revenue systems and coaches leaders; a VP of Sales runs the front-line selling motion day to day. At Series B a fractional CRO often develops or hires the VP of Sales rather than being one.

### Should a Series B company hire a fractional CRO or a full-time VP of Sales first?
It depends on the gap. If the problem is systems, forecasting, and org design, a fractional CRO fits. If you already have a working motion and just need someone to run and grow the team daily, a full-time VP of Sales may be the better first hire.

### What metrics should you hold a fractional CRO accountable to?
Forecast accuracy, pipeline coverage, sales cycle and win-rate trends, rep ramp time, and the readiness of the team to operate without them. Personal bookings matter less than whether the revenue machine becomes predictable and self-sufficient.

## FAQ

**What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?**
A fractional CRO carries operational accountability for the revenue number and manages the revenue team, embedded in your cadences and board prep. A consultant delivers recommendations and typically has no ongoing ownership of outcomes or people.

**Is Series B too early for any kind of CRO?**
No. Series B is often the ideal moment because the company has product-market fit but lacks a repeatable, forecastable revenue engine. Fractional is frequently the right first form of the role because the function is still being invented.

**How many days a week does a fractional CRO typically work?**
Commonly one to three days per week, depending on the mandate and stage. Confirm the actual commitment in writing, and be wary of leaders spread thin across many simultaneous clients.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO engagement is working?**
Within 90 days you should see a documented sales process, a more trustworthy forecast, clearer pipeline visibility, and a visibly improving sales team. If the only output is decks and meetings, the engagement is underperforming.

**Should the fractional CRO help hire their full-time replacement?**
Yes — this is one of the strongest signals of a good engagement. A well-structured fractional CRO designs the permanent role, sets the scorecard, and often helps recruit and onboard their successor, ensuring continuity rather than a cliff.

**What industries or motions matter most when matching a fractional CRO?**
Match on go-to-market motion first — product-led versus sales-led, self-serve versus enterprise, deal size and cycle length — and on stage second. Vertical industry familiarity helps but rarely outweighs a mismatch in motion or stage experience.

**Can a fractional CRO work if the founder is still leading sales?**
Yes, and it is common. Part of the mandate is transitioning revenue leadership off the founder's plate by building systems and developing leaders, so the founder can step back from being in every deal without revenue stalling.
